thread_title: S. leucophylla var. alba Baldwin Co, AL clone A
breadcrumb: S. leucophylla var. alba Baldwin Co, AL clone A

posts.body_html:
Here's an interesting clone of S. leucophylla var. alba that has more white than your average, every-day S. leucophylla. With the younger summer traps, there are veins on the interior of the trap, but during the fall, it can become completely white. Another interesting facet of this clone is the amount of white on the trap. Normally, especially during the spring and summer, the white pigment doesn't go below the mouth too much. The amount of white seen on the summer traps on this clone is about the same as the amount of white you'd normally see on a fall pitcher of a "regular" clone. Can't wait to see if the fall traps on this plant produce some extreme white pitchers!

Last year, this plant dried up (I didn't water the plant enough and the next day, there was a heat wave) and also fried in a heat wave. As if there wasn't enough damage already, the wind threw a couple of punches at it and kicked it a couple of times, causing the amazing yet beat up trap to toppled over. Long story short: even though the trap showed some outstanding characteristics, I didn't end up photographing it. In fact, many of my outstanding S. leucophylla clones were burnt last year, but hopefully, I'll be able to photograph and share them with you all this year.

All the baby'ing afterwards paid off, as this one is producing some neat looking traps. photos were taken 5/31/14.


notice the sunburn on other neighboring plants. This is a struggle we have every year when there's random early season heat waves:



Yes, that is a crazy amazing red variant in the background, and hopefully, the fall pitchers won't be fried so that they can be photographed:

posts.body_html:
Leucophyllas always make me nervous about this time of the year...will they produce fall traps, or are they already going dormant? It seems when we consistently have warmer weather, all the plants produce a strong set of fall traps, but if we get cold snaps and lots of cloudy days in the late summer/early fall, it triggers the plants to go dormant early. So far, it seems like one or two of the hurricane creek white divisions produced fall traps about 2 months early, but the rest of the plants are only producing either nominal summer traps or phyllodia. S. leucophylla var. alba MKL042, one of my favorite bright white clones, seems like it has already gone dormant! fingers crossed it's still active because it didn't produce dit-a-lee squat this year...

So what's S. leucophylla var. alba Baldwin Co, AL clone A doing? It recently produced 2 impressive pitchers (although it looks more amazing in person than in the photo). Are these the fall pitchers, and that's it, or will there be an even more impressive fall show? Well, the next set of leaves seems to be phyllodia, but that doesn't mean there's a chance for an even more impressive show.

Photos taken 8/1/14-hoping this can get even more white:



Indeed, there are still veins in the interior of the trap, but these were absent last year. Vein patterns are highly environmentally induced, which makes me scratch my head when it comes to all this new nomenclature:

posts.body_html: My leucos are acting "weird" this year too Mike. Last year they acted "normally" that is they just sat there doing nothing in August making me wonder if they were going to do anything at all. Then BAM like clockwork at the very beginning of September they initiated a massive pitcher flush that was active and trapping bugs by mid September. This year some plants are super early but each seems to be on it's own schedule: Purple Lips already has a set of thick fall traps open; HCW A has some OK pitchers open/in the works but not sure if they're "the" fall pitchers; HCW F and HCW unknown clone aren't doing anything yet; AJ01 has massive traps in the early stages; Alabama hasn't done anything yet; Tarnok is chilling; random super vigrorous leuco is producing traps but not sure if they are the fall ones. Our weather here has been cool-ish - high 70s low 80s with plenty of foggy mornings. I do hope we get a couple good heat waves in the next 30 days - last year the leucos grew like bamboo when it was in the 90s! We'll see!

posts.body_html:
Calen, you're back! You married yet or what brohamz?! LOL

Thanks for sharing your observations, such data is really important to document, and I'm constantly fascinated by realizing how little we know about S. leucophylla pitcher production.

I checked some posts from last year, and around mid to late September, I had the large fall pitcher flush on the leucos. This implies that in the next 2 weeks, if there aren't any large traps starting to emerge from the growth point, either the fall show will be delayed or not present this year. Our temperatures are in the 50's at night and low 80's during the day, so maybe this might be slowing them down. all else equal, it seems like warm days and warm nights, especially during the fall, increases the probability of large pitcher production.

Rob Co had a S. leucophylla 'Alabama' plant in June of this year produce large traps for him, but he's in a greenhouse. Outdoors for me, that clone has NEVER produced big spring/summer traps.

One thing that really impressed me in the FL bogs was how robust the spring pitchers were on the leucos. posts.body_html:
Hi Mike,
We are experience something very similar with many of our leucos as well. Pitchers are up early, but it seems like some of the plants (like our Purple Lip x self clone 2)are going back to producing phyllodia. This particular plant produced a flurry of pitchers a couple of weeks ago and then stopped, and its sibling is now sending up big traps. Other leucos are sending up pitchers too. This is early for us, and we are in the middle of the "mean season" down here in south Florida--nights are upper seventies and days are mid nineties. Usually the leucos are resting, and don't start with pitchers until late Sept.-Oct.
We are south of their habitat where conditions are more tropical, and we're experiencing something similar to you, living north of their typical habitats. We've talked to other growers living in the "Sarracenia Belt" who are having this occur too.
Go figure...

Interesting sunbelle!

It's official: my leucos are going for it about two weeks earlier than last year. A lot has happened since I posted several days ago - strong pitchers have emerged and are growing like wildfire from plants that were quiet 5 days ago! It's crazy how the leucs just spring into action. There are just two plants in my collection - HCW Clone F and Titan - that still seem to be holding back. Fingers crossed the F in particular throws up some nice traps!
